gist: Five Lawfare contributors whose careers were built by 9/11 — including a former FBI agent, a former CIA officer with five Iraq tours, a former military officer turned law-of-armed-conflict lawyer, and Lawfare founder Benjamin Wittes — argue that the post-9/11 security state accelerated pre-existing trends rather than creating new ones, and that several of its authorities have now outlived their purpose. The most operative claims are that DHS is behind the bulk of indefensible national security actions of the past 18 months, that counterterrorism-era law-of-war interpretations are being stretched onto boat strikes and nation-versus-nation conflict, and that the 2001 AUMF and presidential emergency authorities should be systematically reviewed or repealed.

insights.claim: The post-9/11 national security state was not created on 9/11 but accelerated four pre-existing trends: treating international terrorism as a military rather than law enforcement problem, expanding covert action including renditions, hardening critical infrastructure, and building out surveillance capacity and its legal architecture.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes, Lawfare
insights.so_what: If the security architecture reflects long-run structural trends rather than one shock, expecting it to unwind on an anniversary or with a change of administration is a category error.
insights.quote: 9/11 radically accelerated a set of trends that were already underway

insights.claim: The idea that the US answers al-Qaeda with Tomahawk cruise missiles rather than domestic criminal process is a creature of the late Clinton administration, and the AUMF passed days after 9/11 merely accelerated that existing posture.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes, Lawfare
insights.so_what: Attributing the militarization of counterterrorism to a single statute understates how durable the underlying policy consensus is and how hard reversal would be.
insights.quote: that sense that, you know, you use Tomahawk cruise missiles to deal with al-Qaeda is a creature of the late Clinton administration

insights.claim: The most durable institutional gain from 9/11 was cultural rather than statutory: analysts and operators abandoned agency-by-agency stovepiping voluntarily once the mission shifted from post-hoc explanation to prevention, a change described as an almost unqualified good.
insights.speaker: Michael Feinberg, former FBI
insights.so_what: Information-sharing culture, not reorganization, is what actually changed after 9/11, which suggests future reform effort is better spent on incentives than on org charts.
insights.quote: the atomized way of doing things agency by agency was no longer really going to work if you were going to shift from a posture where you were dealing with the contingency of a big war

insights.claim: A second lasting cultural effect was that surveillance authorities, special operations units and intelligence tradecraft moved from an insider professional conversation into mainstream public discourse and popular media, a shift driven as much by how media responded to 9/11 as by the attack itself.
insights.speaker: Michael Feinberg, former FBI
insights.so_what: Public salience of national security law is itself a post-9/11 artifact, and it is what makes today's domestic deployment and surveillance fights politically contested rather than technocratic.
insights.quote: In the pre-9/11 era, outside of a very specific sort of group of professionals and practitioners, you know, surveillance authorities weren't really something that took up a lot of ink in most newspapers.

themes.theme: DHS as the Institution That Outlived Its Purpose

insights.claim: The Department of Homeland Security is the post-9/11 institution most clearly past its original purpose, having been created as a coordinating reorganization of thematically unrelated agencies and evolved into a catch-all agency that duplicates other law enforcement capabilities.
insights.speaker: Michael Feinberg, former FBI
insights.so_what: A former federal agent arguing publicly for unwinding DHS signals that institutional-reform pressure is building from inside the national security community, not only from civil libertarians.
insights.quote: DHS 100%. DHS was a reorganization based on increasing administrative efficiencies between disparate organizations that were not necessarily tied together thematically, but didn't fit anywhere else.

insights.claim: The overwhelming majority of indefensible law enforcement and national security actions over roughly the past 18 months have come from DHS rather than from older agencies, because DHS lacks the accumulated institutional history of mistakes and correction that constrains organizations like the FBI.
insights.speaker: Michael Feinberg, former FBI
insights.so_what: Institutional age and scar tissue, not formal legal limits, are the real brake on agency misconduct, which identifies newer agencies as the highest-risk actors to watch.
insights.quote: the overwhelming majority of what I will call indefensible law enforcement or national security actions over the past 18 months or so have been largely done by DHS and not by some of the older, more staid organizations

insights.claim: Organizations reliably solidify and expand their own power over time regardless of their founding charter, which is why a coordinating body like DHS drifted into an operational agency with its own enforcement capabilities.
insights.speaker: Michael Feinberg, former FBI
insights.so_what: Applied prospectively, any newly created coordinating authority should be assumed to become an operational one, which argues for sunset clauses at creation rather than review after the fact.
insights.quote: organizations tend to solidify their power as much as they can

themes.theme: Law-of-War Interpretations Migrating to New Conflicts

insights.claim: Counterterrorism-era modifications to the law of armed conflict, particularly the expansive and unweighted definition of membership in an organized armed group under the law of war manual, are now being applied to boat strikes and potentially to other countries, which would collapse the foundations of the law of war when mapped onto nation-versus-nation conflict.
insights.speaker: Lauren Voss, former military officer and attorney
insights.so_what: This is the concrete legal mechanism by which counterterrorism authorities become a template for interstate force, and it is the framework to watch as strikes on non-state targets expand geographically.
insights.quote: At this At the point you start talking about membership in this amorphous way is this point you start talking about economics as being something you can target when you're it's nation versus nation

insights.claim: The war-sustaining targeting doctrine, which permitted striking economic activity such as drug trafficking that financed a terrorist group, does not translate to state-versus-state conflict and there is currently no good proposal or solution on offer for constraining its spread.
insights.speaker: Lauren Voss, former military officer and attorney
insights.so_what: If economic targets become lawful by analogy to counterterrorism finance, the escalation ladder in any future great-power confrontation starts much lower and commercial actors become targets.
insights.quote: there's also this argument around war sustaining that made sense in a counterterrorism context of, you know, if if this economic thing, like drugs for example, is is sustaining the terrorist group, that can indeed be targeted.

insights.claim: The counterterrorism toolkit is now being opened against domestic categories of people by designating criminal groups as terrorists, enabling lethal operations against individuals engaged in what would otherwise be non-capital activities, and by adding groups such as pro-transgender Americans to intelligence collection priority frameworks.
insights.speaker: Julia Kerley, former CIA
insights.so_what: Terrorist designation is becoming a general-purpose legal unlock, which means designation announcements are the leading indicator for where lethal and surveillance authorities will next be applied.
insights.quote: being a part of an apparatus that's now uh wantonly making criminal groups into terrorists so that it opens up a CT toolkit to do lethal operations against people engaged in non-capital activities.

insights.claim: The 2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force should be repealed outright, with no good remaining reason for it to be law or to be authorizing anything 25 years after its passage.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes, Lawfare
insights.so_what: AUMF repeal is the single cleanest legislative lever over the geographic scope of US military operations and remains a live congressional fight.
insights.quote: The first of them is the authorization for the use of military force of 2001. There is no good reason why this should still be law

insights.claim: All presidential emergency authorities, spanning both post-9/11 and pre-9/11 statutes, warrant significant review, amendment and in some cases outright repeal, because in the current environment the authorities themselves are more dangerous than the threats they were written to counter.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes, Lawfare
insights.so_what: Emergency powers are the mechanism through which unilateral executive action gets legal cover across domains, so any systematic review would have wide policy and market consequences.
insights.quote: We are living in an environment right now in which the authorities themselves are more dangerous than the than the things that they allow the president to protect against.

insights.claim: The repeal case is framed as a two-sided error rather than a one-sided one: people are alive today because these authorities existed and were used as intended, and people have died because they were later withdrawn, so the honest argument is that they have outlived their necessity rather than that they were always wrong.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes, Lawfare
insights.so_what: Framing repeal as a periodic review problem rather than a moral indictment is the version most likely to attract bipartisan support, which raises the odds it eventually happens.
insights.quote: you can err in both directions here, and we have erred in both directions.

insights.claim: A former CIA officer who credits Section 702 and other counterterrorism authorities with saving lives, including possibly her own, now favors effectively rescinding those same authorities on the grounds that wars wrap up and even justified capabilities should be revisited.
insights.speaker: Julia Kerley, former CIA
insights.so_what: When practitioners who used and benefited from 702 publicly support rescission, the coalition for surveillance reform widens beyond its traditional civil-liberties base ahead of future reauthorization fights.
insights.quote: there are people alive because of the CT authorities, because of the 702 authorities. People alive, including I think myself, because of the authorities and capabilities that we were able to use in a war-fighting context.

insights.claim: There is no regular institutional process for revisiting whether counterterrorism authorities and capabilities are still needed, which is why they persist long past their justification and are now being abused.
insights.speaker: Julia Kerley, former CIA
insights.so_what: The absence of a sunset-and-review mechanism, rather than any single bad statute, is the structural failure, and it is the design flaw most likely to recur in any new emergency framework.
insights.quote: I wish there was a more regular process for revisiting these things.

insights.claim: A former FBI agent who spent years dismissing civil libertarian warnings that expanded surveillance and administrative warrant powers would be turned on American citizens now says those critics were 100% correct, because the drafted restrictions failed once officials with no respect for norms took power.
insights.speaker: Michael Feinberg, former FBI
insights.so_what: The operative lesson is that statutory safeguards depend entirely on the good faith of the officeholder, which means legal text is a weak predictor of how any new authority will actually be used.
insights.quote: what I've seen now is that when people take power who have no respect for norm or balance, like the civil libertarians I brushed off were 100% correct.

insights.claim: The institutional backbone of agencies like the FBI, CIA and the military did not hold the line when powers intended to combat terrorism were redirected to other purposes, contrary to the assumption practitioners made when those powers were granted.
insights.speaker: Michael Feinberg, former FBI
insights.so_what: If internal agency culture is not a reliable constraint, external checks, courts and disclosure become the only meaningful guardrails, which raises the value of litigation and oversight as forecasting signals.
insights.quote: we were really wrong about the institutional backbones of those organizations and that they would hold the line when pressed to use powers intended to combat terrorism to do something else instead.

insights.claim: The critics who warned about future abuse of national security authorities should not be dismissed as histrionic, but they also were not responsible for keeping Americans safe, did not have access to threat information, and did not come with solutions, so both roles are necessary parts of the same conversation.
insights.speaker: Natalie Orpett, Lawfare
insights.so_what: This is the steelman that makes surveillance reform coalitions durable, and it is notable that the dissenting side explicitly declines to claim vindication.
insights.quote: although a lot of my concerns have proved justified, I am not taking a victory lap

insights.claim: Government institutions are not monoliths, with significant documented internal tension between the FBI and CIA particularly in the Guantanamo context, which complicates any account that treats the national security state as a single actor.
insights.speaker: Natalie Orpett, Lawfare
insights.so_what: Interagency friction is a real source of internal check and of leaks, and it is where reform efforts and policy reversals often originate.

insights.claim: Lawfare founder Benjamin Wittes distinguishes between authorities he still supports in principle and their corrupted application, saying he believes in drone strikes but not against fishermen, and in robust surveillance authorities but not for pursuing political enemies.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes, Lawfare
insights.so_what: The reference to strikes against fishermen ties the abstract debate directly to current maritime lethal operations, signaling where the sharpest legal contestation is now focused.
insights.quote: I believe in drone strikes. I don't believe in drone strikes against fishermen. I believe in surveillance authorities that are relatively robust. I don't believe in using them to go after political enemies.

insights.claim: Lawfare itself exists only because of 9/11, having grown out of a Washington Post opinion writer's pre-existing but unusual background in national security law, which became a full-time institutional focus at Brookings within five years of the attacks.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Wittes, Lawfare
insights.so_what: The entire specialist national security law commentary ecosystem is a post-9/11 creation, which explains why its practitioners are now the loudest voices on domestic deployment and emergency powers.
insights.quote: Lawfare absolutely certainly would not exist but for 9/11.

insights.claim: Recruitment into the national security workforce after 9/11 ran on a sense of calling rather than career economics, with tens or hundreds of thousands treating protection of strangers as a life purpose, and in at least one case the GI Bill was the only route from a working-class background into law school and a Pentagon policy career.
insights.speaker: Lauren Voss and Michael Feinberg
insights.so_what: A workforce built on mission identity rather than compensation is unusually vulnerable to disillusionment, which is a real attrition risk for agencies whose missions are now being repurposed.
insights.quote: dedicate your life to the safety of strangers is a calling that is more rewarding than I can ever articulate

insights.claim: The Afghanistan withdrawal remains an unresolved operational and moral liability, with the Special Immigrant Visa program covering only immediate family and forcing evacuees to choose between leaving unmarried siblings behind under Taliban rule or staying, and with volunteer organizations still doing the work years later.
insights.speaker: Lauren Voss, former military officer and attorney
insights.so_what: SIV program scope is a concrete, unfinished policy failure with an identifiable constituency, and it is the kind of narrow fix that periodically resurfaces in legislation.
insights.quote: we had people with unmarried sisters who were going to, you know, leave have to leave them behind knowing what the Taliban might do, but we're, you know, fearful for their own children.
